messages:
alex_support: Customer reporting intermittent 429s on our text-generation endpoint since yesterday afternoon. They say their org quota is barely used (about 45%), but clients get 429 in spikes. Attached sample response headers and curl below.

maria_support: can you drop the org id + project + api key prefixes (redact tokens) and the request_id from the response? also which region? will triage. :eyes:

alex_support: Org: org_ACME (redacted). Project: proj-inbox (redacted). Region: us-west-2. request_id: r-001a2b3c. Here is the curl and response:

```
curl -i -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-REDACTED" -d '{"input":"hello"}' https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate
```

HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
X-RateLimit-Limit: 60
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0
X-RateLimit-Reset: 1798512400
Retry-After: 25
X-Quota-Scope: ip_burst
X-Limit-Rule: ip_burst_1m

alex_support: Note: customer says they rotate multiple API keys from different projects in the same org (dev apps + prod), and all traffic goes through their corporate proxy so the upstream IP is a small pool.

sam_eng: hmm. that X-Quota-Scope header is interesting — backend is tagging this as an IP burst rule not the api-key rule. Means the per-IP bucket fired before per-key.

maria_support: have they ever hit per-key limits? any historical 429s tied to api keys?

alex_support: they have sporadic key-limited events but not matching timestamps. This is purely spikes when dozens of clients warm up.

jin_prod: quick primer: we enforce multiple limit dimensions in order of evaluation: API key -> project -> IP -> org (but IP can short-circuit if burst threshold is exceeded). Also we have an adaptive burst guard that aggregates by upstream IP + network label for NATed proxies. In this case, if many rotated keys share same source IP, the IP bucket can be consumed very fast.

alex_support: can we confirm that our proxy preserves X-Forwarded-For? customer says proxy sets X-Forwarded-For to client IDs but upstream only shows proxy IP.

sam_eng: that matters. The rate limiter uses the immediate peer IP by default unless we see a trusted `X-Forwarded-For` from a whitelisted proxy. If their proxy isn't on our trusted list, traffic collapses to a small set of IPs.

maria_support: action items: 1) ask customer to send the raw request_id + timestamp window (we have r-001a2b3c at 1798512350), 2) run internal log query to find which rule matched, 3) propose mitigation.

alex_support: running the query now: `GET /internal/logs?request_id=r-001a2b3c` -> result: `limit_match: ip_burst_1m`, `matched_bucket: 10.11.22.33/32`, `bucket_owner: unknown-proxy`, `current_count: 135`, `limit: 120`.

ops-bot: deploy-bot: observed transient spike on us-west-2 inference fleet at 1798512348, autoscale handled compute but no change to rate-limit state.

jin_prod: that log confirms: IP bucket (10.11.22.33) exceeded the 1-minute burst cap. Even though per-key usage low, aggregate caused 429s.

maria_support: ok let's prepare options for customer: 1) identify and whitelist their proxy IPs so we use X-Forwarded-For; 2) apply a temporary org-level higher burst allowance; 3) advise rotating to a single long-lived key per client behind the proxy to spread across api-key buckets rather than aggregate on IP.

alex_support: customer asked "why does IP take precedence over api-key?" They see keys tied to projects and think api-key should be the primary guard.

sam_eng: internal note to explain: precedence is by evaluation order but short-circuiting IP burst reduces our exposure to sudden distributed bursts from many keys on same NAT — otherwise one rogue network could amplify by rotating keys. But we should document precedence clearly.

maria_support: I'll draft a response to customer with repro steps. Draft below — please edit: 

"Hi — thanks for the report. We traced the 429s to an IP-based burst guard (X-Quota-Scope: ip_burst). Because many clients behind your corporate proxy share the same external IP, the IP-level bucket was consumed quickly even though individual API keys were under quota. Workarounds: a) add your proxy IPs to our trusted proxy list (support will give details), b) use longer-lived keys per client so requests distribute across per-key buckets, or c) request a temporary org burst increase from support while you remediate. We can also run a one-off mapping to see which keys/prefixes contributed to the spike. Let us know which option you prefer"

jin_prod: small add: include command to pull trace: `curl -H "X-Request-ID: r-001a2b3c" https://internal.redwood.ai/debug/limits?org=org_ACME` — will show which rule matched and the bucket key.

alex_support: sent to customer, they replied they can whitelist proxy but it's managed by IT and needs approval (2–3 days). They asked for a short-term fix.

maria_support: I approved a 24h org-level burst increase, and flagged bill-impact to finance (small). I also created a ticket to add better visibility in Console for "dominant limit cause" so customers can see which dimension triggered the 429.

sam_eng: follow-up engineering items: 1) ensure X-Quota-Scope header is present in all 429s (it was missing sometimes in old flows), 2) add docs about precedence and trusted proxy config, 3) consider adding a per-org override for NAT-heavy customers.

alex_support: customer confirmed 429s stopped after org-burst increase. They will pursue proxy whitelist and key consolidation. Closing after 48h observation. :white_check_mark:

maria_support: thanks everyone. I'll convert this thread into a KB article for support and link to docs. :memo:

sam_eng: filing eng follow-ups: ENG-3912 (console visibility), ENG-3913 (trusted-proxy UX), ENG-3914 (ensure X-Quota-Scope on 429s).

jin_prod: nice teamwork. keeps coming back to NAT and proxy patterns as common pitfall.

alex_support: closing in 48h unless customer reopens. :lock:
